content: The Aqua Detox device is marketed as a tool for detoxification, which involves immersing an individual’s feet in a saline solution while an electrical current is passed through the bath. This device is said to be based on the research of Royal Rife. However, it has faced criticism for potentially misleading consumers. The device, or similar versions of it, is sold under various brand names, as the original company behind Aqua Detox provides web design services to resellers. As of October 15, 2006, the Aqua Detox brand became part of a new parent company called The Agenta Group. The manufacturer of Aqua Detox claims that the system generates positive and negative ions, which purportedly resonate through the body and stimulate cellular activity. This process is said to rebalance cellular energy, enabling cells to function more efficiently and expel toxins that have accumulated in the body’s tissues. According to the manufacturer, using the device for 20 to 35 minutes every two to three days can result in the excretion of toxins through the 2,000 pores located on the feet. However, the manufacturer has not provided evidence to substantiate these detoxification claims, though it asserts that a clinical trial is underway to validate the device’s efficacy. Despite the manufacturer not explicitly claiming that Aqua Detox can treat or cure diseases, the device has been scrutinized by the British Advertising Standards Authority (ASA). On April 6, 2005, the ASA ruled against Aqua Detox International for using customer testimonials that implied the device was effective in treating serious diseases. The ASA also challenged the general efficacy of the device. Both complaints were upheld, and the company agreed to remove the misleading testimonials from its advertisements. One marketer, Miracle Beauty, claims that the color changes in the footbath water indicate which areas of the body have been detoxified. For example, black water is said to represent toxins from the liver, orange from the joints, and green from the gallbladder. However, the device uses iron electrodes that corrode during the process, producing rust that turns the water brown when the saline solution is electrolyzed. Variations in water color can be attributed to differences in the amount of salt added to the solution and the composition of the electrodes. Experiments have demonstrated that the water changes color regardless of whether feet are placed in the bath, suggesting that the color change is unrelated to any detoxification process. For instance, an experiment using salt water and a car battery showed that the water’s composition remained the same whether or not feet were present. Critics, such as Dr. Stephen Barrett, argue that the Aqua Detox device is merely performing electrolysis, with the rusting of the electrodes being misrepresented as evidence of toxin removal. The color change in the water is used to mislead consumers into believing the device is effective. Furthermore, the Aqua Detox device has not been evaluated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Marketing materials for the product include a disclaimer stating that it is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.
